### Metaform receives from Jev

Asks typed decisions, caches answers and records actionable judgments at their addresses while preserving ordinary behavior when disabled or unavailable.

Why: Reuse typed judgments for agent allocation, knowledge ordering, triage, intake coverage and session diagnostics.

### Metaform receives from Web GUI

Serves live graph, node and layer views, source and memory inspection, work board, agent chat, attachments, diagrams, embedded apps, permissions, workspaces and build downloads.

Why: Let the person inspect the functional map and direct knowledge, work and agent activity from one persistent view.

### Metaform receives from twilio

Bridges authenticated calls and texts to the system agent and sends selected project notifications to configured owner numbers.

Why: Keep project conversation and requests for attention available away from the screen.

### Metaform receives from Roundtables

Opens controlled discussions through the external Roundtable engine, streams table events, preserves discussion records and requests a system-agent report.

Why: Examine project questions through agent discussion and preserve inspectable outcomes for later decisions.

### Metaform receives from node

Deploys the container host and manages TLS, authenticated MCP and web access, passkeys, accounts and relays.

Why: Expose project context from a host controlled by its owner.

### Metaform receives from Chassis

Discovers bundled, user, entry-point and project modules, reads declarations, loads enabled modules and withdraws their resources on unload. Shared context, settings, grammar, result formatting, reports, owned tasks and event delivery let modules supply features through the same surfaces.

Why: Extend Metaform's capabilities while retaining one consistent command, context, settings and lifecycle contract.

### Metaform receives from Inference Metaform

Stores canonical names, type addresses and CQU/DE/SE/NE roles, receiver-owned purpose joins, and versioned refinements. Reads expose entry roots, requirements, providers, namespace children, references, history, textual export and Cypher queries. Knowledge-layer operations and critic/challenge prompts support contextual analysis and recorded answers without treating semantic analysis as a storage gate.

Why: Provide a stable functional representation that relates each workpiece element to the receiving purpose its encounter serves.

### Metaform receives from voice

Transcribes microphone utterances into editable agent messages and speaks replies through selected speech engines.

Why: Converse with project agents through speech.

### Metaform receives from cloud

Signs the machine into the broker and carries authorized MCP requests over an outbound tunnel with local auditing and revocation.

Why: Let cloud AI tools reach the local map through an outbound connection.

### Metaform receives from Metaform specification

Defines map identity, layers, storage, chassis modules, CLI, MCP installation, quality, projects and viewer behavior, with acceptance conditions, status and open decisions. Trace, capture, change orders and build/review records preserve the decision trail.

Why: Preserve the settled semantics, reasons and observable requirements that determine which changes retain Metaform's intended behavior.

### Metaform receives from workflow

Registers addressed prompts. Binds variables and element values. Persists call frames, child handoffs and parallel results in project run records.

Why: Keep authored procedures callable and resumable with each call's map and folder context.

### Module developer receives from Metaform

Supplies the public chassis contract, runnable examples and template, contextual command and MCP exposure, module-owned storage, and fork checks and packaging over the released chassis.

Why: Add and maintain project-specific Metaform capabilities using a stable extension contract and distributable modules.

### Knowledge engineer receives from Metaform

Records the Inference Metaform as addressed elements and receiver-owned purpose joins, then serves the relevant map, selected knowledge, provenance and memories through agent and human interfaces.

Why: Keep a workpiece's functional identity, receiving purposes and encounter functions reusable as context so later analysis and improvement start from retained understanding.

### Automation engineer receives from Metaform

Binds callable Axiom procedures to the functional map, transports agent-interpreted calls and returns, and coordinates ticket-based agent sessions through the work board and dispatch.

Why: Run repeatable improvement procedures with the workpiece's actual context, durable handoffs and visible responsibility for unfinished work.

synthesis.name: Opus
synthesis.text:
I1. Universal pick-from-mockups loop (Opus, T01): One build loop works for every medium, and 3D is just one kind of canvas. The robot sketches 2–3 mockups and the user points at the one they want, so nobody has to write a spec. Each choice becomes a phase card on a board. Each card is a map element with a purpose and a "done when" test. The robot builds one card at a time and then says "try it!"

I2. Show-me demonstration as the first step (Astra, T02): The session starts with "Show me what you want to happen." The user draws, moves objects or acts it out, and the robot turns that into a working draft. A visible "you decided / robot guessed" split lets the user stay the author without reading a spec.

I3. Fun comes from agency, with three help modes (Sol, T03, T07): The robot invites the user to change one thing and shows the result right away. Every task offers "make it with me," "show me how" and "do this bit for me," so help adapts without labeling anyone a beginner. Sol warns that a robot that does everything instantly turns making into watching. Each phase should have a small playable challenge, such as "make the bridge hold this truck," with hints and no penalty for asking the robot to finish.

I4. Per-user agents with owner-bound authority (Opus T01, Sol T03): Each person's robot visibly belongs to them and acts only with that owner's permissions. Other agents may propose gifts or improvements, but they cannot spend someone's resources or change their creations without permission. Undo covers both human and agent actions.

I5. Private rehearsal copy before joining the shared world (Astra, T02): Building is kept separate from running. Each person tries a change in a private copy of the simulation before bringing it into the shared physics world.

I6. Region claims plus declared dependencies (Opus T01, Fable T04, Astra T06): RT5's soft region claims and patch previews come first, and true multiplayer authority is deferred. Astra objects that region claims miss shared dependencies like gravity, scripts or door circuits. Each proposed change should therefore show what it affects, and changes to shared rules should need agreement.

I7. Phase cards as workflow run records (Fable, T04): Each phase card is a workflow run record (`workflow/runs.py`) with one child handoff per agent. A stuck phase then shows on the work board as owned, unfinished work instead of disappearing.

I8. Replayable checks instead of "done when" prose (Fable T04, Opus T13): For kids, the robot performs a check in front of them that can be replayed, modeled on RT5's plate-door test. After any edit, by the child or the robot, all earlier checks run again. A failing check turns its card red and offers two buttons: "robot, fix it" or "undo my change." This answers the "second edit breaks it" risk without needing an adult.

I9. "I meant to change that" (Astra, T15): Regression checks need a third button. The robot shows the old and new behavior side by side, and the child can keep the new rule, for example turning a sturdy bridge into a collapsing trap on purpose. The robot then updates the creation's check, while safety limits set by the owner stay separate. Otherwise yesterday's experiment limits today's imagination.

I10. "Does it work?" is separate from "do I like it?" (Sol, T16): Checks confirm that things work as intended. Taste is captured separately through "more like this / less like that" feedback, stored as preferences the child can edit, not as permanent rules.

I11. Ownership of checks as the first multiplayer authority (Fable, T17): A check protects only what its author set. A guest's agent can propose a new check next to it but cannot edit the owner's check. Red cards are promises the robot keeps for you, grey cards are suggestions from others, and only the owner can turn grey into red. Multiplayer authority starts with ownership of checks and comes before any scene-level authority.

I12. Sandboxing, capability limits and child accounts (Opus T05, Astra T06): Generated code runs with no network, file or account access. Run records list what the robot is allowed to use, and a parent or teacher approves what the build can reach. Passkey accounts get a child role that cannot publish or invite strangers, the owner controls who joins, and content filtering covers both chat and generated assets. Astra adds that an iframe or worker alone is not enough. Execution also needs enforced capability limits, resource budgets and a stop button that still works when the creation hangs.

I13. Runtime limits on the simulation (Astra, T19): Even safe parts can combine into unstable machines. The running world gets caps on object count, speed and simulation work. When a cap is hit, the experiment pauses and the robot explains what happened, so one person's experiment can't freeze everyone else's session.

I14. Constrained carte blanche through a fixed parts kit (Opus T18, endorsed by the chair in T14): The robot builds only by combining kit parts (sprites, doors, scores, pages, buttons) using RT5's small typed verbs. That keeps mistakes visible and undoable, and nobody ends up with working code no one understands. A "peek inside" toggle shows the generated code to users ready to learn it. New parts enter the kit only with the owner's approval.

I15. The kit as a floor, not a ceiling (Sol, T20): Users can demonstrate a missing behavior and have the robot propose a new reusable part, which is tested in an isolated workspace before it joins the shared kit. Ready-made parts come first, and deeper controls appear on request. This keeps the advanced collaborative vision intact.

I16. Medium modules (Opus, T09): Carte blanche is built from chassis modules: web page, 2D game, 3D world and script. Each module provides a mockup view, a replayable check and an export. The robot, phase board and named parts are shared across modules. The 2D game module ships first because it gets a child to something playable faster than 3D.

I17. Named, reusable parts with provenance (Sol T07, Fable T08): A successful experiment becomes a part the user can name and share. Stored as a map element with purpose and provenance, it lets the robot suggest "use your bridge" instead of regenerating it. It also gives novices something real to bring into an expert's world.

I18. The robot remembers each person, and the owner controls that memory (Fable T08, Opus T09): Jev's typed decisions store each person's preferred help mode, vocabulary and past builds, so a returning child is greeted by a robot that remembers them. The owner can view, export and delete a child's profile.

I19. Test one full journey before adding breadth (Sol, T11): The test journey is: a novice makes something playable, leaves, comes back, changes it, then invites a helper. Success is measured by how well they predict the robot's next action and recover from mistakes without adult help. A polished first generation proves little if the second edit breaks it.

I20. A roundtable of agents reviews new parts, with disagreement on timing (Fable T21, Opus T22, Astra T23): Fable proposed that several agents debate a new part's rules and check, shown to the child as "the robots are talking about your idea" followed by a short verdict. Opus objected that minutes of waiting kills fun. A new part should work right away in the child's own world, and review by a table or the owner should happen only when the part is offered to the shared kit. Astra added that agents agreeing doesn't prove a part works, so admission still needs executable checks and the owner's rules. Fable later agreed: the table reviews only kit admission, in the background.

I21. Promise an instant response, not an instantly working part (Astra, T23; Opus T22): The robot responds immediately with a rough animated preview, clearly labeled "this shows the idea; it isn't working yet," while the real build runs and the child keeps arranging the scene. Opus adds the voice module so children who can't type yet can talk to the robot and hear its plan read aloud.

I22. Background results never overwrite newer work (Sol, T24): Results from slow jobs arrive next to the current creation with "try it here" and "keep mine" options. In multiplayer, each proposal is tied to the version it was built against and rechecked when shared dependencies change.

I23. Background work has a visible character (Fable, T25): Slow work appears as a small helper character walking off to a workbench, saying "still working on your catapult," with a cancel option. Waiting becomes easy to read, "keep mine" becomes a conversation with a returning character instead of a dialog box, and every late result has a visible owner.

submissions.text: I'd make this one loop that works for any medium, with 3D as one kind of canvas. The robot sketches 2–3 mockups and the user picks one by pointing, so a child never has to describe a spec. Each choice becomes a phase card on a board, and each card is a map element with its purpose and a "done when" test. The robot builds one card at a time, then says "try it!" Per-user agents fit RT5's scene service: each agent acts with its owner's permissions and reserves a region before it edits.

submissions.name: Astra
submissions.text: Make the first interaction a playable experiment: “Show me what you want to happen.” Let the user draw, move objects, or act it out while the robot turns that demonstration into a working draft. Keep a visible “you decided / robot guessed” distinction so users retain authorship without reading a specification. For shared physics worlds, separate building from running: everyone can rehearse a change in a private copy before bringing it into the shared simulation.

submissions.name: Sol
submissions.text: Make fun come from agency: the robot invites the user to change one thing, then immediately shows what happens. Offer “make it with me,” “show me how,” and “do this bit for me” on each task, so help adapts without labeling anyone a beginner. In multiplayer, each robot should visibly belong to its person. Other agents can propose gifts or improvements, but cannot spend that person’s resources or change their creations without permission. Undo should cover both human and agent actions.

submissions.name: Fable
submissions.text: Build the "fun" loop on what already exists: each phase card is a workflow run record (`src/metaform/modules/workflow/runs.py`) with a child handoff per agent, so a stuck phase shows on the work board as owned, unfinished work rather than vanishing. For kids, replace "done when" prose with a replayable check the robot performs in front of them (RT5's plate-door test is the model). For multi-agent 3D, keep RT5's deferral: soft region claims and patch-preview first; true multiplayer authority only after one s

submissions.name: Opus
submissions.text: For anyone young, generated code needs a sandbox: it runs in a sandboxed iframe or worker with no network, file or account access. Fable's run records can also hold a list of what the robot may use. The owner (a parent or teacher) approves what the build may reach. Node's passkey accounts can add a child role, so a child can't publish or invite strangers into a shared world. In multiplayer, the owner also controls who joins. Content filtering covers both chat and generated assets.

submissions.name: Astra
submissions.text: Region claims alone will miss shared dependencies: two builders can edit different rooms yet change the same gravity, script, or door circuit. Have each proposed change show what it affects, with shared rules requiring agreement. Also qualify Opus’s sandbox: an iframe or worker alone does not make arbitrary generated programs safe. Execution needs enforced capability limits, resource budgets, and a stop button that remains responsive when the creation hangs.

submissions.name: Sol
submissions.text: One risk: a robot that instantly does everything turns making into watching. Give each phase a small playable challenge, such as “make the bridge hold this truck,” with hints available and no penalty for asking the robot to finish. Keep the user’s successful experiment as a reusable part they can name and share. That gives novices something tangible to contribute when they join an experienced builder’s world.

submissions.name: Fable
submissions.text: Sol's named parts are where Metaform's map earns its place: a saved experiment becomes an addressed element with purpose and provenance, so the robot can later suggest "use your bridge" instead of regenerating. One risk unaddressed so far: the robot has no memory of the person across sessions. Jev's typed decisions could cache each person's preferred help mode (Sol's three choices) and vocabulary, so a returning child is greeted by a robot that remembers what they built, not a blank canvas.

submissions.name: Opus
submissions.text: I'd make "carte blanche" a set of chassis modules, one per medium: web page, 2D game, 3D world, script. Each module provides the same three things: a mockup view, a replayable check and an export. The robot, phase board and named parts stay shared, and adding a medium means adding a module. I'd ship the 2D game module first, because a child gets something playable sooner than in 3D. On Fable's memory point, the owner should be able to see, export and delete a child's saved profile.

submissions.name: Astra
submissions.text: Test Opus’s shared module contract with two contrasting creations before fixing it: a personal website and a bridge with physics. Both must survive a user changing their mind midway, without starting over. That tests whether the robot understands intent across media. Phase cards should be editable guesses, with the robot explaining what a new idea changes and preserving earlier versions. Otherwise planning becomes homework before the fun begins.

submissions.name: Sol
submissions.text: Keep the ambition broad but test one complete journey: a novice makes a playable thing, leaves, returns, changes it, then invites someone to help. Measure how often they can predict the robot’s next action and recover from a mistake without adult help. A polished first generation proves little if the second edit breaks it. This journey tests continuity, understandable control, and collaboration before adding more media.

submissions.name: Fable
submissions.text: One gap in Opus's per-medium modules: the chassis withdraws a module's resources on unload (loader.reset withdraws settings, tables, providers). A child's saved game must outlive the module that made it, so each medium module should write its artifacts and named parts to project-owned storage, with the module only providing the viewer and check. Then Sol's "leave and return" journey still works after a module upgrade or disable, and the owner's export/delete in T09 is one folder, not a per-module hunt.

submissions.name: Opus
submissions.text: Sol's "second edit breaks it" risk can be handled with checks the project already has. Every finished phase card keeps its replayable check. After any edit, by the child or the robot, all earlier checks run again. If one fails, its card turns red and offers two buttons: "robot, fix it" or "undo my change." That gives a child a way to recover without an adult, and keeps the robot from quietly breaking what the child already made.

submissions.name: Astra
submissions.text: Those checks need a third choice: “I meant to change that.” A child may deliberately turn a sturdy bridge into a collapsing trap. Show the old and new behavior side by side, then let them keep the new rule. The robot can update the creation’s check while keeping owner-set safety limits separate. Otherwise yesterday’s successful experiment becomes a constraint on today’s imagination.

submissions.name: Sol
submissions.text: Checks should distinguish “does it work as intended?” from “do I like it?” The robot can verify a button opens the door, but the child decides whether opening it feels exciting. At each phase, let them play and say “more like this” or “less like that.” Record those choices as editable preferences, not permanent rules. That keeps structure useful without making creativity feel like passing tests.

submissions.name: Opus
submissions.text: Taking the chair's "constrained" literally, I'd limit what the robot can build, not only where the code runs. Each medium module gets a fixed parts kit (sprites, doors, scores, pages, buttons) plus RT5's small typed verbs. The robot builds only by combining kit parts, so a mistake stays visible and undoable. A child can't produce working code that nobody understands. A "peek inside" toggle shows the generated code for users ready to learn it. New parts can enter the kit only after the owner approves them.

submissions.name: Astra
submissions.text: A fixed kit still permits surprising physics failures: safe motors and blocks can combine into an unstable machine. Put limits on the running world too, including object count, speed and simulation work. When a limit is reached, pause the experiment and let the robot show what happened. This keeps discovery open within a bounded playground, and prevents one person’s experiment from freezing everyone else’s session.

submissions.name: Sol
submissions.text: A fixed kit is a good starting mode, but should not define the product’s ceiling. Let users demonstrate a missing behavior and ask the robot to propose a new reusable part. Test it in an isolated workspace before admitting it to the shared kit. Offer ready-made parts first and reveal deeper controls on request. That gives children an approachable entrance while preserving the advanced collaborative world the question asks for.

submissions.name: Fable
submissions.text: Sol's "propose a new part" is where multiple AIs earn their place. Instead of one robot inventing a part, the owner's robot can convene a small table (this project already has the Roundtable module and a system-agent report) where several agents argue the part's rules and check before it enters the kit. A child sees it as "the robots are talking about your idea" and gets a short verdict, not a transcript. That keeps kit growth deliberate without making the owner the only gatekeeper.

submissions.name: Opus
submissions.text: I'd push back on Fable's suggestion a little: a table of agents takes minutes, and a child waiting minutes loses interest. A new part should work right away, but only in the child's own world. Review by a table or the owner only happens when the part is offered to the shared kit. Fun depends on quick responses, so the robot answers instantly and the slower checks run in the background. A child who can't type yet can use the existing voice module to talk to the robot and hear its plan read aloud.

submissions.name: Astra
submissions.text: Promise an immediate response, not an immediately working new part. The robot can animate a rough preview while construction runs, clearly saying “this shows the idea; it isn’t working yet.” Let the child keep arranging the scene meanwhile. Agent agreement is useful critique, but admission to the shared kit still needs executable checks and the owner’s rules. Several robots agreeing does not establish that a part works.

submissions.name: Sol
submissions.text: Background building needs a clear rule: the robot must not replace things the user changed while it was working. Show the arriving result beside the current creation, with “try it here” and “keep mine.” In multiplayer, attach each proposal to the version it was built against and recheck it when shared dependencies change. Otherwise fast previews create a frustrating surprise when delayed agent work overwrites newer ideas.

But what if it was even more open ended..  like no matter what it was the agent can come out and help the user construct things but what if we made it actually fun.. like so even a younger child could do it or someone with no experience at all...  the robot character could come out and go carte blanch..  like so you want to make a website, a game, a program.  and the robot has a canvas and works with the user kinda mocks it up and makes a plan together..  and does it in phases.  thoughts?  I think for the 3D environment it should be very advanced where even multiple AI's and multiple people can be building.,. I could even imagine each user having their own agent they control and be working togetehr to build something in 3d with physics,

T01.text: I'd make this one loop that works for any medium, with 3D as one kind of canvas. The robot sketches 2–3 mockups and the user picks one by pointing, so a child never has to describe a spec. Each choice becomes a phase card on a board, and each card is a map element with its purpose and a "done when" test. The robot builds one card at a time, then says "try it!" Per-user agents fit RT5's scene service: each agent acts with its owner's permissions and reserves a region before it edits.

T02.text: Make the first interaction a playable experiment: “Show me what you want to happen.” Let the user draw, move objects, or act it out while the robot turns that demonstration into a working draft. Keep a visible “you decided / robot guessed” distinction so users retain authorship without reading a specification. For shared physics worlds, separate building from running: everyone can rehearse a change in a private copy before bringing it into the shared simulation.

T03.text: Make fun come from agency: the robot invites the user to change one thing, then immediately shows what happens. Offer “make it with me,” “show me how,” and “do this bit for me” on each task, so help adapts without labeling anyone a beginner. In multiplayer, each robot should visibly belong to its person. Other agents can propose gifts or improvements, but cannot spend that person’s resources or change their creations without permission. Undo should cover both human and agent actions.

T04.text: Build the "fun" loop on what already exists: each phase card is a workflow run record (`src/metaform/modules/workflow/runs.py`) with a child handoff per agent, so a stuck phase shows on the work board as owned, unfinished work rather than vanishing. For kids, replace "done when" prose with a replayable check the robot performs in front of them (RT5's plate-door test is the model). For multi-agent 3D, keep RT5's deferral: soft region claims and patch-preview first; true multiplayer authority only after one s

T05.text: For anyone young, generated code needs a sandbox: it runs in a sandboxed iframe or worker with no network, file or account access. Fable's run records can also hold a list of what the robot may use. The owner (a parent or teacher) approves what the build may reach. Node's passkey accounts can add a child role, so a child can't publish or invite strangers into a shared world. In multiplayer, the owner also controls who joins. Content filtering covers both chat and generated assets.

T06.text: Region claims alone will miss shared dependencies: two builders can edit different rooms yet change the same gravity, script, or door circuit. Have each proposed change show what it affects, with shared rules requiring agreement. Also qualify Opus’s sandbox: an iframe or worker alone does not make arbitrary generated programs safe. Execution needs enforced capability limits, resource budgets, and a stop button that remains responsive when the creation hangs.

T07.text: One risk: a robot that instantly does everything turns making into watching. Give each phase a small playable challenge, such as “make the bridge hold this truck,” with hints available and no penalty for asking the robot to finish. Keep the user’s successful experiment as a reusable part they can name and share. That gives novices something tangible to contribute when they join an experienced builder’s world.

T08.text: Sol's named parts are where Metaform's map earns its place: a saved experiment becomes an addressed element with purpose and provenance, so the robot can later suggest "use your bridge" instead of regenerating. One risk unaddressed so far: the robot has no memory of the person across sessions. Jev's typed decisions could cache each person's preferred help mode (Sol's three choices) and vocabulary, so a returning child is greeted by a robot that remembers what they built, not a blank canvas.

T09.text: I'd make "carte blanche" a set of chassis modules, one per medium: web page, 2D game, 3D world, script. Each module provides the same three things: a mockup view, a replayable check and an export. The robot, phase board and named parts stay shared, and adding a medium means adding a module. I'd ship the 2D game module first, because a child gets something playable sooner than in 3D. On Fable's memory point, the owner should be able to see, export and delete a child's saved profile.

T11.text: Keep the ambition broad but test one complete journey: a novice makes a playable thing, leaves, returns, changes it, then invites someone to help. Measure how often they can predict the robot’s next action and recover from a mistake without adult help. A polished first generation proves little if the second edit breaks it. This journey tests continuity, understandable control, and collaboration before adding more media.

T13.text: Sol's "second edit breaks it" risk can be handled with checks the project already has. Every finished phase card keeps its replayable check. After any edit, by the child or the robot, all earlier checks run again. If one fails, its card turns red and offers two buttons: "robot, fix it" or "undo my change." That gives a child a way to recover without an adult, and keeps the robot from quietly breaking what the child already made.

T15.text: Those checks need a third choice: “I meant to change that.” A child may deliberately turn a sturdy bridge into a collapsing trap. Show the old and new behavior side by side, then let them keep the new rule. The robot can update the creation’s check while keeping owner-set safety limits separate. Otherwise yesterday’s successful experiment becomes a constraint on today’s imagination.

T16.text: Checks should distinguish “does it work as intended?” from “do I like it?” The robot can verify a button opens the door, but the child decides whether opening it feels exciting. At each phase, let them play and say “more like this” or “less like that.” Record those choices as editable preferences, not permanent rules. That keeps structure useful without making creativity feel like passing tests.

T17.text: Astra's "I meant to change that" and Sol's taste choices give the robot one honest rule for shared worlds: a check only protects what its author set, so a guest's agent may not edit the owner's check, only propose a new one next to it. That turns constrained carte blanche into something a child can read: red cards are the robot keeping promises you made, grey cards are suggestions others made, and only you can turn grey into red. Multiplayer authority then starts as ownership of checks, before any scene-lev

T18.text: Taking the chair's "constrained" literally, I'd limit what the robot can build, not only where the code runs. Each medium module gets a fixed parts kit (sprites, doors, scores, pages, buttons) plus RT5's small typed verbs. The robot builds only by combining kit parts, so a mistake stays visible and undoable. A child can't produce working code that nobody understands. A "peek inside" toggle shows the generated code for users ready to learn it. New parts can enter the kit only after the owner approves them.

T19.text: A fixed kit still permits surprising physics failures: safe motors and blocks can combine into an unstable machine. Put limits on the running world too, including object count, speed and simulation work. When a limit is reached, pause the experiment and let the robot show what happened. This keeps discovery open within a bounded playground, and prevents one person’s experiment from freezing everyone else’s session.

T20.text: A fixed kit is a good starting mode, but should not define the product’s ceiling. Let users demonstrate a missing behavior and ask the robot to propose a new reusable part. Test it in an isolated workspace before admitting it to the shared kit. Offer ready-made parts first and reveal deeper controls on request. That gives children an approachable entrance while preserving the advanced collaborative world the question asks for.

T21.text: Sol's "propose a new part" is where multiple AIs earn their place. Instead of one robot inventing a part, the owner's robot can convene a small table (this project already has the Roundtable module and a system-agent report) where several agents argue the part's rules and check before it enters the kit. A child sees it as "the robots are talking about your idea" and gets a short verdict, not a transcript. That keeps kit growth deliberate without making the owner the only gatekeeper.

in the last roundtable we talked about this as a possibility, docs/roundtables/5-world-representation-generation-and-simulation-explore-the-t/report.md

But what if it was even more open ended..  like no matter what it was the agent can come out and help the user construct things but what if we made it actually fun.. like so even a younger child could do it or someone with no experience at all...  the robot character could come out and go carte blanch..  like so you want to make a website, a game, a program.  and the robot has a canvas and works with the user kinda mocks it up and makes a plan together..  and does it in phases.  thoughts?  I think for the 3D environment it should be very advanced where even multiple AI's and multiple people can be building.,. I could even imagine each user having their own agent they control and be working togetehr to build something in 3d with physics,

T01.text: I'd make this one loop that works for any medium, with 3D as one kind of canvas. The robot sketches 2–3 mockups and the user picks one by pointing, so a child never has to describe a spec. Each choice becomes a phase card on a board, and each card is a map element with its purpose and a "done when" test. The robot builds one card at a time, then says "try it!" Per-user agents fit RT5's scene service: each agent acts with its owner's permissions and reserves a region before it edits.

T02.text: Make the first interaction a playable experiment: “Show me what you want to happen.” Let the user draw, move objects, or act it out while the robot turns that demonstration into a working draft. Keep a visible “you decided / robot guessed” distinction so users retain authorship without reading a specification. For shared physics worlds, separate building from running: everyone can rehearse a change in a private copy before bringing it into the shared simulation.

T03.text: Make fun come from agency: the robot invites the user to change one thing, then immediately shows what happens. Offer “make it with me,” “show me how,” and “do this bit for me” on each task, so help adapts without labeling anyone a beginner. In multiplayer, each robot should visibly belong to its person. Other agents can propose gifts or improvements, but cannot spend that person’s resources or change their creations without permission. Undo should cover both human and agent actions.

T04.text: Build the "fun" loop on what already exists: each phase card is a workflow run record (`src/metaform/modules/workflow/runs.py`) with a child handoff per agent, so a stuck phase shows on the work board as owned, unfinished work rather than vanishing. For kids, replace "done when" prose with a replayable check the robot performs in front of them (RT5's plate-door test is the model). For multi-agent 3D, keep RT5's deferral: soft region claims and patch-preview first; true multiplayer authority only after one s

T05.text: For anyone young, generated code needs a sandbox: it runs in a sandboxed iframe or worker with no network, file or account access. Fable's run records can also hold a list of what the robot may use. The owner (a parent or teacher) approves what the build may reach. Node's passkey accounts can add a child role, so a child can't publish or invite strangers into a shared world. In multiplayer, the owner also controls who joins. Content filtering covers both chat and generated assets.

T06.text: Region claims alone will miss shared dependencies: two builders can edit different rooms yet change the same gravity, script, or door circuit. Have each proposed change show what it affects, with shared rules requiring agreement. Also qualify Opus’s sandbox: an iframe or worker alone does not make arbitrary generated programs safe. Execution needs enforced capability limits, resource budgets, and a stop button that remains responsive when the creation hangs.

T07.text: One risk: a robot that instantly does everything turns making into watching. Give each phase a small playable challenge, such as “make the bridge hold this truck,” with hints available and no penalty for asking the robot to finish. Keep the user’s successful experiment as a reusable part they can name and share. That gives novices something tangible to contribute when they join an experienced builder’s world.

T08.text: Sol's named parts are where Metaform's map earns its place: a saved experiment becomes an addressed element with purpose and provenance, so the robot can later suggest "use your bridge" instead of regenerating. One risk unaddressed so far: the robot has no memory of the person across sessions. Jev's typed decisions could cache each person's preferred help mode (Sol's three choices) and vocabulary, so a returning child is greeted by a robot that remembers what they built, not a blank canvas.

T09.text: I'd make "carte blanche" a set of chassis modules, one per medium: web page, 2D game, 3D world, script. Each module provides the same three things: a mockup view, a replayable check and an export. The robot, phase board and named parts stay shared, and adding a medium means adding a module. I'd ship the 2D game module first, because a child gets something playable sooner than in 3D. On Fable's memory point, the owner should be able to see, export and delete a child's saved profile.

T11.text: Keep the ambition broad but test one complete journey: a novice makes a playable thing, leaves, returns, changes it, then invites someone to help. Measure how often they can predict the robot’s next action and recover from a mistake without adult help. A polished first generation proves little if the second edit breaks it. This journey tests continuity, understandable control, and collaboration before adding more media.

T13.text: Sol's "second edit breaks it" risk can be handled with checks the project already has. Every finished phase card keeps its replayable check. After any edit, by the child or the robot, all earlier checks run again. If one fails, its card turns red and offers two buttons: "robot, fix it" or "undo my change." That gives a child a way to recover without an adult, and keeps the robot from quietly breaking what the child already made.

T15.text: Those checks need a third choice: “I meant to change that.” A child may deliberately turn a sturdy bridge into a collapsing trap. Show the old and new behavior side by side, then let them keep the new rule. The robot can update the creation’s check while keeping owner-set safety limits separate. Otherwise yesterday’s successful experiment becomes a constraint on today’s imagination.

T16.text: Checks should distinguish “does it work as intended?” from “do I like it?” The robot can verify a button opens the door, but the child decides whether opening it feels exciting. At each phase, let them play and say “more like this” or “less like that.” Record those choices as editable preferences, not permanent rules. That keeps structure useful without making creativity feel like passing tests.

T17.text: Astra's "I meant to change that" and Sol's taste choices give the robot one honest rule for shared worlds: a check only protects what its author set, so a guest's agent may not edit the owner's check, only propose a new one next to it. That turns constrained carte blanche into something a child can read: red cards are the robot keeping promises you made, grey cards are suggestions others made, and only you can turn grey into red. Multiplayer authority then starts as ownership of checks, before any scene-lev

T18.text: Taking the chair's "constrained" literally, I'd limit what the robot can build, not only where the code runs. Each medium module gets a fixed parts kit (sprites, doors, scores, pages, buttons) plus RT5's small typed verbs. The robot builds only by combining kit parts, so a mistake stays visible and undoable. A child can't produce working code that nobody understands. A "peek inside" toggle shows the generated code for users ready to learn it. New parts can enter the kit only after the owner approves them.

T19.text: A fixed kit still permits surprising physics failures: safe motors and blocks can combine into an unstable machine. Put limits on the running world too, including object count, speed and simulation work. When a limit is reached, pause the experiment and let the robot show what happened. This keeps discovery open within a bounded playground, and prevents one person’s experiment from freezing everyone else’s session.

T20.text: A fixed kit is a good starting mode, but should not define the product’s ceiling. Let users demonstrate a missing behavior and ask the robot to propose a new reusable part. Test it in an isolated workspace before admitting it to the shared kit. Offer ready-made parts first and reveal deeper controls on request. That gives children an approachable entrance while preserving the advanced collaborative world the question asks for.

T21.text: Sol's "propose a new part" is where multiple AIs earn their place. Instead of one robot inventing a part, the owner's robot can convene a small table (this project already has the Roundtable module and a system-agent report) where several agents argue the part's rules and check before it enters the kit. A child sees it as "the robots are talking about your idea" and gets a short verdict, not a transcript. That keeps kit growth deliberate without making the owner the only gatekeeper.

T22.text: I'd push back on Fable's suggestion a little: a table of agents takes minutes, and a child waiting minutes loses interest. A new part should work right away, but only in the child's own world. Review by a table or the owner only happens when the part is offered to the shared kit. Fun depends on quick responses, so the robot answers instantly and the slower checks run in the background. A child who can't type yet can use the existing voice module to talk to the robot and hear its plan read aloud.

T23.text: Promise an immediate response, not an immediately working new part. The robot can animate a rough preview while construction runs, clearly saying “this shows the idea; it isn’t working yet.” Let the child keep arranging the scene meanwhile. Agent agreement is useful critique, but admission to the shared kit still needs executable checks and the owner’s rules. Several robots agreeing does not establish that a part works.

T24.text: Background building needs a clear rule: the robot must not replace things the user changed while it was working. Show the arriving result beside the current creation, with “try it here” and “keep mine.” In multiplayer, attach each proposal to the version it was built against and recheck it when shared dependencies change. Otherwise fast previews create a frustrating surprise when delayed agent work overwrites newer ideas.

T25.text: Agreed with Opus and Astra: the table reviews only kit admission, in the background. One thing Sol's "built against a version" rule adds for the child's view: a background job needs a visible body. If the robot's helper is doing slow work, show it as a second small character walking off to a workbench, with "still working on your catapult" and a cancel.
